Let us pause and reflect a little on these words. ' I recollect the day when the power and the name of Englishmen were hateful to my heart.' Here is the accumulated bitterness of ages and centuries of oppression. That was the condition of John Dillon, that was the condition of the Irish people-bitterness of heart caused by the odious manner in which they had been treated for ages and centuries. But the fact that at that time a great party was ready to come to the relief of Ireland was enough to take away the bitterness from the heart of John Dillon. He was applauded by the people of Ireland. Therefore, I say, trust the people of Ireland, let them be treated kindly, let them be treated fairly, let them be treated justly, and the bitterness will pass away and they will become the most loyal subjects in the British empire. I am not taking too sanguine a view. There is example and justification of my words in the language I have just quoted from John Dillon. But, so long as you continue to give to the people of Ireland, from time to time, simply a scanty measure of what they would expect, you will not make them contented and happy. If there is on the face of the earth, a generous people, a warm-hearted people, never slow to resent an injury, but never slow to be grateful for a favour received, it is the Irish people; and, for my part- I do not wish to speak at length on the subject, for it has been well threshed out -I do not believe that if this question is to be solved, it can only be by giving the Irish people the measure of liberty that we have in Canada, and to give them, not the powers we have in the parliament of the confederation, but the powers we give to the provinces. Let there be a parliament on College Green. Let the heart and mind of the Irish people be appealed to, and Ireland, instead of being, as in the past, a thorn in the flesh of England, will become a tower of strength to the British empire.

Mr. Speaker, before the vote is taken, I desire

to say a few words. I regret that I was not able to hear the whole of the debate. It did seem to me that when my hon. friend from Victoria, N.B. (Hon. Mr. Costigan) gave notice of his resolution that this was a somewhat inopportune time to introduce it. What is regarded as a very liberal measure of relief with respect to one question which has agitated Ireland for some time, has been introduced by the English government. For that reason, possibly, the occasion for the introduction of this resolution is not of the happiest. Also, I think that the resolution is not very happily worded. I should have thought that my hon. friend from Victoria, N.B'., might perhaps have couched his thoughts in the concluding clauses of the resolution in some happier terms. I think all of us in this House desire that every possible measure of relief be given to Ireland in respect of any grievance which she has sustained in the past or from what she now suffers ; but at the same time we do not desire to place ourselves in a position which is not a dignified one. I would like to call the attention of my right hon. friend to the concluding words of this resolution :
We have observed, may it please your Majesty, with feelings of profound satisfaction the evidence afforded in the debate of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom, and in the speech from the Throne, of a sincere desire on all sides to usher in a new era of lasting peace and good will.
I would like to submit to my right hon. friend whether after all it is a very dignified, not to say a pertinent, thing for us to discuss the tone of a debate in the imperial House of Commons. It does not seem to me that the resolution is worded in the best way in that regard. We might have it followed by a proposed resolution of this House with regard to the eloquence of some speech of a British cabinet minister, or of a member of the House of Commons, and we would not be going very much beyond the length to which we are asked to go in this resolution. However, that is a matter of form more than a matter of substance; and I would have been inclined, if I had been favoured to any extent with the confidence of the hon. gentleman who moved this resolution, to suggest to him, as well as to my right hon. friend who is responsible for the dignity as well as the proceedings of this House, that the resolution might have been amended in that respect and yet be just as serviceable to the cause of home rule.
Now the resolution seems to be somewhat unhappily worded in another regard. It refers to a measure which is about to be introduced into the British House of Commons. Well, since the notice was given, since the address was drawn up, that resolution has been introduced, and criticism might fairly be made I think on the terms of the resolution that it hardly does justice to the present circumstances.

But apart from this, Mr. Speaker, I listened with a good deal of attention to the very able speech of my hon. friend from Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), and I thought there was a good deal in it worthy of consideration by all of us in this House. At the same time we cannot disguise from ourselves the fact that not only with regard to home rule in Ireland, but with regard to other matters of imperial concern, we have in the past taken upon ourselves to make suggestions to the imperial government. As to the wisdom of that course, there may be more than one opinion, as to the service or value of it, there may be more than one opinion. I really do not know whether the cause of home rule in Ireland, the redress of grievances under which Ireland has suffered in the past, has been materially aided by any resolution or by any action of the Canadian House of Commons. It is quite true that we passed a resolution unanimously some three years ago with regard to the cause of our fellow subjects in South Africa. But I think the House should not forget that that resolution was followed up by active and material assistance when the cause of our fellow subjects there came to be decided by the force of arms. It is a fair question for hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House as to what extent we should take upon ourselves to tender advice in imperial matters where we are not prepared to supplement that advice by some active and material assistance.
Now I would like to call the attention of my hon. friend the mover of this resolution to the fact that there are communities in Canada at the present time which are demanding that same measure of home rule which he is demanding for Ireland. I am referring to the people of the North-west Territories of Canada, who, by the unanimous resolution of their representatives in the territorial legislature, have called upon this government, nearly two years ago, to grant to them exactly the same rights which are possessed by the people of all the provinces of Canada. Perhaps it might be a fair matter of consideration as to whether those claims and those demands should not engage our attention during this session, and whether our time might not at least be equally devoted to them as well as to the claims of our fellow countrymen in Ireland.
With regard to what my right hon. friend has said respecting the cause of home rule in Ireland, I am happy to say that a great deal of it commends itself to my judgment, but I do not altogether think that the cause of home rule, or the success of home rule, will be reached in the way he appears to believe. I think that home rule, not only to the Irish people but to the people of all the British islands, will come in the future, and come perhaps in the very near future, from the very necessity of things. We know how utterly inadequate is the time at the command of the imperial House of Commons

for consideration of the great subjects which come before that House. I myself have sat in the gallery of the House of Commons at Westminster and seen the affairs of India, a country of 300,000,000, disposed of In a single evening, and with not more than one-fifth of the membership of the House present. We know that during the past two or three years estimates, items amounting to $25,000,000, have been passed through the imperial House with a discussion of only an hour or two, for the reason that the time of the House was so taken up with a multitude of other matters that it was absolutely impossible to devote to these subjects the time they really demanded. Now, whether by an extension of the power of county councils in the mother country, whether by the establishment of district councils, or by the establishment of local parliaments of some kind, I believe that that condition of affairs must be relieved, and will be relieved in the very near future.
In the meantime, however, a very great measure has been proposed to the imperial House of Commons, a measure which is an object lesson to the whole world. A country that has spent hundreds of millions in asserting the rights of her subjects in South Africa, now presents to the world the spectacle of granting as a loan in the first instance $500,000,000 or $600,000,000, accompanied with a vote of $60,000,000 to $70,000,000 for the purpose of relieving a portion of the United Kingdom from a grievance which has existed for a great many years past. That is a great measure, it is a measure that is worthy of the parliament of a great country. Whether or not it will have all the success which most of us believe and hope it will have, certainly we must all recognize that it is an intelligent and sincere step in the direction of ameliorating the grievances from which Ireland has suffered in the past. Therefore, I say that all of us join with our fellow countrymen on the other side of the water in trusting that that measure may pass, and that it may have the result which we all hope for. That Ireland is worthy of an effort of this kind none of us will deny. My right hon. friend has said that he believes that Ireland will be loyal. I go beyond that: I say that I believe Ireland is and has been loyal to the British Crown, notwithstanding these grievances from which she has suffered in the past. When I speak of Ireland I speak of the great mass of the people of Ireland, and I have the battlefields of the empire to justify me in saying that Ireland has been loyal and devoted to the Crown of the United Kingdom in all of the years past. Go to the thousand battlefields of the empire, look where the charge has been fiercest in the hour of victory, or where the foe has pressed nearest in the hour of retreat, on every one of these battlefields Ireland may claim and has claimed her glorious dead, the dead who have fought and bled for the welfare of the empire. Not only has Ireland done this, but Ireland has given to the empire men in every rank of life who have contributed much to the upbuilding of the empire and to the cause of civilization. Therefore, I say. Mr. Speaker, that I do not accept the suggestion that Ireland will be loyal in the future ; I say that the mass of the Irish people, the great body of the Irish people have been loyal in the past to the empire, and are loyal at present to the empire, and this I say to their credit, because, during all these years they have been oppressed with a sense of wrong and injustice, and they have felt that they have not been fairly treated. Notwithstanding that, they have stood side by side and shoulder to shoulder with their brethren in Scotland and England, and they have been devoted and loyal to the cause of the empire in every walk and department of life.
Now, there is another striking circumstance in connection with the present measure that has been brought forward in the House of Commons, and that is the fact, from which I draw a good omen for the future, that Irishmen throughout Canada, and I believe Irishmen throughout the United Kingdom, are impressed with the belief that the present attitude of the British government is to a large extent, to a considerable extent, at least, due to the personal influence of our most gracious Sovereign. I draw from that a very happy omen for the future, because the tie which binds Ireland, as well as Canada, to the empire, the tie of allegiance to the Crown, is only a technical tie, and while it is only a technical tie it has no very great strength. It requires something stronger and deeper than that. The belief that Irishmen entertain throughout Canada and throughout the mother country as to the effect of the personal influence of our Sovereign will, I believe, strengthen that tie so that it will become enduring and imperishable so that Ireland not only will remain loyal but will become the most loyal portion of His Majesty's dominion throughout the world. That, Sir, is a very happy circumstance indeed. That is a circumstance which we welcome on this side of the Atlantic, and a circumstance which, I am sure, will render the future of the United Kingdom of much happier omen than the conditions of the past might have justified us in expecting a few years ago. Now, I do not know that I have anything to add. As I said before, I think that the precedents that we have had introduced in regard to Ireland herself, and the precedent which we established in 1900 in regard to our fellow countrymen in South Africa, justify us in voting for this resolution, although I am bound to say that I would have preferred that it should have been introduced at some more opportune moment, and (that it should have been

couched in some happier terms. Therefore, for these reasons, by reason of the precedents of the past, in the hope that this may in some measure strengthen those in the United Kingdom who brought forward this measure, and in the belief that, acting upon these precedents of the past, we have no other course to follow at the present time, I, speaking for myself, now declare my intention of voting for this resolution.
Mr- J- SHERRITT (North Middlesex), Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to give a silent vote, nor do I wish to delay the House by the remarks which I have to make. I shall endeavour not to detain the House for more than a minute or two. I am not here to discuss the question of home rule for Ireland ; neither am I here to say the Irish people have not a grievance, nor will I take up the time of the House in establishing the fact that I am in sympathy with Ireland. I am an Irishman myself, and it would not be a very difficult matter for me to establish the fact that I am in sympathy with Ireland, but when we consider that in 1882 we met with a rebuff at the hands of the imperial government, when a motion similar to that now proposed was sent to Great Britain, it does seem to me that we cannot, except that the conditions there have changed so materially in the twenty-one years which have elapsed since that time, that we will not leave ourselves open to receiving another such rebuff as we got at that time. I do not wish to put myself on record as being willing to invite a rebuff of that kind. Under these circumstances I intend to vote against the motion. It is not that I have any feeling against the Irish people, nor is it that I do not represent that class of people. I have the honour to represent a very large number of people of Irish parentage resident in my riding. I am glad to say that the people I represent are intelligent enough to know that any action we may take here will not accomplish very much in their behalf, remembering, as they do, the reception given to the resolution which was sent over twenty-one years ago. For that reason, and that reason only, I intend to vote against this motion if the mover and seconder insist upon the matter being brought to a vote.

Mr. speaker, I do not care to give a vote on this question without explaining my position. I remember that a few years ago I gate a vote in favour of the motion moved by the hon. member for Victoria, N.B. (Mr. Costigan). At that time, I was in favour of anything that could be done in the interest of Ireland, and I am in favour of it now. I am of Irish descent and I would like everything done that would assist that portion of the empire. But, Sir, at the present time I intend to vote against this resolution and I will give my reasons. It sur-

prises me that I have not seen any agitation in this country by the Irish people either Protestants or Catholics asking for any resolution to be introduced in this House in favour of home rule for Ireland, and what is still more surprising to me is that the Irish people of this country of the same religion as the hon. member for Victoria, N.B. (Hon. Mr. Costigan), could not find some leading member of this House, a member of the government, who would introduce it and who would in my opinion add to the credit of the resolution. We have in this House the hon. Minister of Justice, a creditable Irishman, and if the Minister of Justice would introduce a resolution of this kind and explain it, I conceive that a great many more would support it. But here is the hon. member for Victoria, N.B., who has been travelling on this resolution since he was first a member of this House thirty or forty years ago. I believe that this resolution was introduced by the hon. member for Victoria, N.B. (Hon. Mr. Costigan) each and every time for the purpose of booming himself hi the House and so far as I am concerned I do not intend to boom him any more. I believe that a great many men in this House have been speaking here to-night simply for their constituents; simply for the purpose of trying to put themselves in such a position that they may come back to the House again.
I care not whether I come back or not, I intend to express my feelings as I am doing now. I do not believe that it is in the interest of the Irish people of Canada, I believe it was introduced in the interest of the hon. member for Victoria, N.B., and I shall not support any motion which is submitted here for the purpose of serving the ends of any one member. Under these circumstances I feel that I would not be doing myself or my constituents justice if I sat here without explaining the reasons why I shall vote against the resolution. I am sincere in what I say. Is it not a strange thing, Mr. Speaker, that in this House, where we have so many prominent Irishmen, men who are respected from one end of this Dominion to the other, that there is not one of them that will get up here and move the resolution except the hon. gentleman who has been playing with it so long. For that reason I shall vote against it now and every time so long as it is moved in the spirit in which it has been moved to-day.

I venture to intrude in this debate, expressing the hope that nothing which I may say, will mar the effect produced by the very eloquent and statesmanlike utterance we have heard from the Prime Minister.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: Hear, hear.

In corroboration of what the right hon. gentleman lias said, if I may call it corroboration, I would like to read to the House the words

used by the Hon. George E. Foster at the time the Transvaal resolution was introduced here, and I think these words have a very close application to the subject now before us. Mr. Foster said :
These resolutions, I think, are timely, then, because they say to our own British fellow-citizens, who are Uitlanders in the republic, that they have the sympathy and the good will of the British empire as a whole, in all its parts, in their struggle for equal rights. No taxation without representation is a cry to which the world rises, and it will rise in the Dutch republic just as surely as the sun rises. Outside of that, I think, great good will come from the introduction and passage of a resolution like this in that it is another proof of the solidarity of the British empire throughout the world, that to-day, in these times of telegraph wires, and steamships, and quick transmission of intelligence, evokes a lively and sympathetic and deep interest in every part of the British empire in the local fortunes of every other part of the British empire.
It seems to me that this language may very well be taken to heart by hon. gentlemen opposite who are opposed to this resolution. I would ask them to realize that all we ask is that there may be extended to our fellow-countrymen in Ireland, that measure of sympathy and support that two years ago we were asked to extend to the Uit-landers in South Africa. Beyond that we do not go; beyond that, so far as I am concerned, I would not venture to go.
Some hon. gentlemen have taken it upon themselves to discuss the motives and the objects which my hon. friend (Mr. Costigan) had when he moved this resolution. I would be remiss in my duty, if, speaking here tonight, I did not say a word in support of that hon. gentleman, and give expression to the sentiments that I entertain for him. Let me say in this connection that I do not affect to speak for the Irish Catholics of the Dominion of Canada. I have no mandate; no authority to speak for them. I speak to-night, as has been my habit in the past, in the capacity of a Canadian representative of a Canadian constituency, but at the same time I cannot forget that I am an Irish Catholic, and I speak as one of that class (if not for them) when I say that no man in Canada deserves better of the Irish Catholics than the Hon. Mr. Costigan.
Hear, hear.

The Hon. Mr. Costigan enjoys the exceptional advantage of having occupied a seat in this House continuously since confederation, and during that long record he has not done anything that we need blush for. On the contrary, we give our sanction and our approval to all that he has done in so far as Irish Catholic interests are concerned.
Mr. HUGHES (Victoria, Ont.) It is Irish interests he is looking after, not Irish Catholic interests.

I did not quite catch what my hon. friend has said.
Mr. HUGHES (Victoria, Ont.) He is looking after Irish interests, not after Irish Catholic interests.

Yes, lie is looking after Irish interests, and that is what we are dealing with now. The attack made upon the Hon. Mr. Costigan was under the suggestion that his object here was merely to catch votes, and I am referring to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Costigan) with the object of refuting the statement that such is his object. My hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) was good enough to suggest that he would like to challenge any man in this House to say that there was such a thing in existence as an Irish grievance. Well, the answer to that challenge of his was given by the leader of the political party to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes) belongs; but if further answer be required, I could read from the speeches delivered by the Rt. Hon. Mr. Chamberlain as far back as 1885 and 1886. Here is one of the declarations that Mr. Chamberlain had to make on that subject :
It is not a new problem, this Irish question. Once in ten years ; once in twenty years it may be ; sometimes with sufficient warning, sometimes without the slightest preparation like a bolt from the blue sky, the Irish question is upon us. Every generation in turn for 400 years has had to deal with it. Each has disposed of it for a time according to its fashion, and each has had to bequeath it still unsettled
to its successor	Force has been
tried during all this period, and has failed. Nothing is more certain than that force, although it may temporarily have produced order and tranquillity, has left Ireland always as discontented as before, has left the problem still unsolved	The majority of the farmers of Ireland and their families are at the mercy of the ten thousand landlords in the country, and they have suffered much in the past. 'Well, I have nothing to say, and will not say one single word against the Irish landlords as a class. The proof that they have been, on the whole, just and even generous is to be found in the fact that they continue to exist. The occasional enforcement of their rights by an unjust and harsh landlord here and there was enough to cause alarm and indignation throughout the whole district, and was a constant and fruitful source of disaffection in the country ; and when the bad times came-when famine stared these people in the face, and when to every man was brought the possibility of eviction and expatriation-I say it is no wonder that under such circumstances a common danger united the people, induced them to listen to baleful counsels, and occasionally impelled them to criminal deeds.
Now, the question of Irish grievances, it seems to me, is not one that should be discussed here. We all know that Irish grievances have existed, and we know that some exist still. At the same time, I would not be true to my duty if I did not bear testimony to the fact that an honest effort has been made by the English people to remedy those grievances, and I am satisfied that the day is not far distant when the last

of them will have disappeared. In the meantime, what are we called on to do 1 To express onr continued belief in the advantages of the principle of self-government; to say, as the Canadian parliament said in 1882 and again in 1887, that in the light of the experience we have had in Canada, we believe that the principle of selfgovernment when applied to Ireland will have the same result that it has had when applied to Canada. It is not necessary for me to go over the record and point out the advantages which we have enjoyed in Canada as a result of the application of the principle of self-government. Itj is not necessary for me to go over the records since 1837 and point out to this House, the majority of whom are more familiar with the details than I can profess to be, how a change has| come over the spirit of our dream in Canada; how from a country in open revolt, we have come to be a country whose loyalty is unquestioned, and which is looked on to-day as one of the finest countries in the world. We have developed along the lines of self-government, and can it be pretended for one moment that, as the ties have lessened until to-day we have become a nation within a nation, the bonds have in any respect been weakened ? On the contrary, as the ties have been lessened, as the principle of self-government has been developed, the bonds have become firmer; because we now realize what British constitutional liberty means; because we now realize that the British flag stands to us in Canada for liberty, self-government and justice-in a word, for all those things which in the past have been denied to the Irishmen in Ireland.
Now, a large and important portion of this country is interested in this question. It is all very flue for some hon. gentlemen to rise up in this House and say that they love the Irish, they admire the Irish, they recognize the services the Irish have rendered to the empire and to Canada; but that which is more important, it seems to me, than all that is that these hon. gentlemen should show their good will, not by words, but by deeds.
And I cannot agree with those who say that they vote against this resolution, not because of its intrinsic merits, but because it happens to be proposed by an hon. member who does not meet favour in their eyes. It has been suggested, I think by the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Bro-der), that this resolution does not cover the same ground as the resolution of 1882-that it does not contain within it the same restrictions with respect to the rights of the minority in Ireland. My hon. friend never read the resolution, or he would understand that it is a mere reaffirming of the principles of the resolution of 1882, nothing more, nothing less.
On the other hand, some hon. gentleman Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
has said :	We do not wish to obtrude our
opinions on the British House of Commons, because in 1882, when we ventured to offer some suggestions in this respect, we were told by the Earl of Kimberley practically to mind our own business. Well, so Car as I am concerned, I deny to any British statesman, however eminent his position may be, the right to dictate to the Canadian parliament whether or not it has the right to pass a resolution or to petition. That is a right inherent in the Canadian parliament; and, as Sir John Thompson said, and as Mr. Edward Blake said in 1887, oar duty is to deny the right of any English statesman to lay down such a doctrine. But independent altogether of this observation, I would like to say that I appeal lo Mr. Gladstone, better informed in 1887 than he appears to have been in 1882. In 1882 he was the head of the government, and of course was responsible for what the ICarl of Kimberley said when he wrote the letter that has been referred to in the course of the present debate. But Mr. Gladstone in 18S7 received a resolution passed by the provincial legislature at Quebec in favour of his Home Rule Bill, and publicly thanked the legislature for having passed the resolution. We were told that we ought not to obtrude our views on the imperial parliament, because, forsooth, it might occur to the imperial parliament to give us advice-to say, for instance, that the tithe system existing in the province of Quebec should not be tolerated any longer, but should be altered. My hon. friends need not trouble themselves about that. The imperial parliament, if it desired to make any observations in that respect, would not limit itself to observations; it might tomorrow pass an Act to wipe out the whole of those restrictions. The British parliament has the inherent power to amend every line of the British North America Act, and to-morrow the whole British North America Act might be wiped out. But is it likely to occur ? Is it likely, after England has had the experience which she has had of the development of local institutions in Canada, that the imperial parliament would venture to do anything of the sort ? There is no use of creating bugbears for the purpose of putting an argument of that sort before this House.
Now, I would like to say one word as to the other branch of the resolution, that is, the branch that has reference to the question of land tenure in Ireland. I agree, and I am glad to bear testimony to the fact, that there is probably but one people in the world generous enough to deal with a question of this sort, as the English people are attempting to deal with it at the present time. But what are we asked to do ? We are asked to congratulate them practically on what they are doing, to wish them success in their efforts, and bid them God-speed on the road on which they have

entered. Now, is it not right that we should do so ? Never has there been in the history of Ireland anything approaching the conditions that exist to-day. You have, on the one hand, Mr. Redmond, who represents the Nationalist party, rising in his place in the English House of Commons and saying :
The situation in Ireland. was very strange. It was so full of hope that it contained a menace of danger. Crime was unknown, coercion had been suspended, class animosities for the moment were at an end, and united Ireland stood at the bar of that House and asked for the concession of this great measure of justice and appeasement. To raise up the hopes of a whole people to the highest pitch of expectation and then dash them to the ground would be neither a safe nor a sane proceeding. Never in the history of that House had a government had a more blessed opportunity of carrying to fruition a great and blessed policy.
These are the words that fell from the lips of the leader of the Irish Nationalist party. What do we find on the other side? We find Col. Saunderson, who represents the north and who speaks for the landlord element, saying on the same subject:
Ireland was ready to accept this gift, not only for its own benefits, but for the good of the state; and to disappoint the country in the matter would be, in his judgment a crime. He had always held that the purchasing out of the landlords of Ireland was not so mue l for the good of the tenants or the landlords themselves as for the good of the state in con tributing to the general security of the British Empire, by restoring peace, prosperity and contentment to Ireland.
That is the measure rye ask you to approve of. That is the measure to which this House is asked to wish Godspeed. It is a measure which has united all parties in Ireland as they never have been since the repeal of the Union. In the words of my right hon. leader, a unique opportunity lias come to have this difficulty settled. If it was important for us to interfere in the South African matter, it is doubly important that we should interfere at the present juncture in connection with the affairs of Ireland. It is important that we should do so, not only from the standpoint of Canada, but of Ireland and England. Is it not important to have a contented and peaceful Ireland at the doors of England, is it not better to have that country a bulwark and a rampart of the empire, instead of having it as heretofore a hot-bed of revolution and rebellion ? * Any expenditure which will bring about that condition of things, will be an expenditure made in the interests of the empire. As the hon. gentleman who introduced the Bill said, it is an expenditure by which the English exchequer will be enriched, and which will effect a benefit, in so far as the external relations of the empire are concerned, that will have a far more reaching effect than any shadowy attempt to increase the militia or the army in England.
My hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) spoke of the demagogues in the United States who played on the sentiments of the Irish people there. There again we find an additional reason for having this matter settled, because the demagogue would soon be out of business if there were no Irish grievances. He would soon cease to be able to twist the tail of the British lion if Irishmen in America were satisfied that England had done justice to their fellow countrymen at home. I shall not speak about the qualities of my race. Testimony has been borne to their good qualities tonight. But since the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) has been good enough to say that my countrymen have shown their valour on many a well fought field, I may claim that this should dispel any ill-will against Ireland aroused by its unfortunate manifestations of sympathy with the Boers. If you have this sympathy on the one hand, on the other hand you have the valour and the cheers of the Irish soldiers on the veldt in South Africa, which more than once turned the scale when victory trembled in the balance, and gave courage, sympathy and support to the English and Scotch soldiers on the same field. After all the law of compensation must tell, and it seems to me the time is opportune for us to set aside personal feelings, and not stop to consider whether the resolution has been introduced by one hon. gentleman or another, but simply look at the question from the standpoint of Canadians. We should only ask ourselves this question : Is it good for Canada that this resolution should be introduced and adopted ? Is it good for the empire ? Is it for the best interests of Canada and the empire that Ireland should be made peaceful, happy and contented ? The descendants of Irishmen form an important element in this country. Whether our fathers or our grandfathers were born on the old soil, whether we belong to the second or third generation-and I speak as one of the latter-we feel as sincerely aud earnestly for the cause of Ireland to-day as ever did our ancestors in the old land. Surely it is a remarkable and significant fact that men should carry through three successive generations the insatiable desire to have justice done the land from which they hail. We may have never seen the old land, our fathers may never have seen it, but still we hope for the day when all the grievances of Ireland may be settled, and when Irishmen at home will do for England what the Irishmen of Canada are doing for England in this Dominion.

I shall not occupy the attention of the House, Mr. Speaker, many minutes in the few remarks I have to offer on the amendment placed in your hands by the hon. member for Victoria (Hon. Mr. Costigan). But in view of what has been presented to the House on both sides of the question to-

night, I feel that before a vote is taken I should give some reason why I am constrained to vote against the resolution. I listened with a great deal of attention to all that the hon. gentleman had to say, as well as to what fell from the lips of the hon. gentleman who seconded the resolution (Mr. Hackett), and I must sincerely congratulate both those hon. gentlemen on the moderation which characterized their arguments in its support. I am not one of those who find fault with the mover of the resolution for the course he has taken. In view of the diploma he has just received from the hon. the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick), according to which he is looked upon as the representative leader of the Irish people in Canada, he had the right to take the course he did. But I may be permitted to express an opinion, as an Irishman, not representing anybody but myself on this occasion, and an Irishman who belongs to the minority, or at any rate who comes from the stock of the minority in that country. And my opinion is that at this particular time, when a great effort is being made by Protestants and Catholics to solve one of the burning questions which has kept them apart in the motherland, it is highly inexpedient to introduce a resolution dragging this home rule business into the arena. The hon. gentleman knows that the minority in Ireland to-day are as strongly and as irrevocably opposed to home rule, as defined by those authorized to speak for the home rule party in the imperial parliament, as they were ten or even twenty years ago. I repeat, as an Irishman, earnest in his desire to see every grievance existing in the old land removed, this resolution is inexpedient. It will not promote the cause of home rule. It will not redound to the advantage of those who desire to see Ireland, north and south, east and west, united, happy, prosperous and contented. I regret exceedingly that this resolution has been moved and I regret it for these reasons. I regret it because, as the hon. Minister of Justice has pointed out, there is to-day a coming together, there is a meeting of the extremes upon the great measure which a Unionist government-a government which is the result of the attempt of Mr. Gladstone to pass a home rule measure through the imperial parliament-has had the courage, the temerity to bring forward as a solution of a much vexed question. I say I regret very deeply that, at this particular juncture, this unfortunate resolution should be brought in, because the representatives of the north have been shown by the hon. Minister of Justice as agreeing with the representatives of the south-Col. Saunderson agreeing with some other gentleman whose opinion was quoted -that e'verything should be done to secure the passage of that measure through the House of Commons. Now, let me say one word more with regard to the introduction of this resolution. Those who differ from the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Costigan) Mr. CLARKE.
have no right to complain of want of courtesy. They do not expect to receive more than a reasonable measure of courtesy or consideration from the hon. gentleman when he introduces his resolution. iBut we think, and we have a right to think from what has been said by the hon. member for West Prince (Mr. Hackett), that, though he is certainly as enthusiastic as the hon. member for Victoria in his advocacy of home rule for Ireland, he was treated with scant courtesy by the mover of this resolution. The hon. member for West Prince declared on the door of the House that only one hour before he rose to move the resolution did the hon. member for Victoria intimate to him that he was expected to second it. Does not that give some force and effect to the suggestion offered here to-night that, probably-and I would not like to make the statement believing it to be true, but it has been made here -some other consideration than that of the best interests of Ireland moved the hon. gentleman in bringing in his resolution at this time and under these peculiar circumstances ?
It has been pointed out that resolutions were passed by this House dealing with this matter in 1882, 1886, 1897 and 1901. But it has not been stated that since these resolutions were passed, since the parliament of Canada first placed itself on record respecting the granting of a measure of home rule to Ireland, the matter has been dealt with by the imperial parliament, the parliament whose duty it is to legislate for England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales, the parliament best capable of dealing with the interests of the people of the United Kingdom. That parliament has dealt with this question of home rule on two occasions since 1882. The first occasion was in 1886, when the late Itt. Hon. W. E. Gladstone introduced a Bill. He was defeated, and he succeeded in breaking the Liberal party in two, and the pieces have not been brought together to this day. That right hon. gentleman introduced the measure again in 1893, carried it through the popular assembly, but it was defeated in the House of Lords. So, on the two occasions when the question of home rule came within the field of practical politics, when the representatives of the estates were given an opportunity to speak upon it, they declared against it. And I say-and I think I say it advisedly-that it ill-becomes us to offer an opinion and give advice when those whose duty it is to deal with this matter have, on two occasions, expressed their opinion and given advice to the Sovereign as to what is best to be done in the interests of the people of the United Kingdom. Sir, the present Unionist government owes its existence to the attempt on the part of the Liberal party, headed by that great statesman, the late Mr. Gladstone, to give home rule to Ireland. The Liberal party was smashed and the Liberal-Unionists withdrew because of their disagreement with
