their leader upon this question. But since this Unionist government came into power, whose members were pledged against home rule, they have given the strongest and best proofs that could be given to the Irish people, as well as to the Irish race all over the world, that they do not desire to see any real grievance in Ireland remain unredressed. They have given abundant proofs of their desire to remove every real grievance. They have passed two Land Acts since they came into power. They have passed a local government Bill which has practically revolutionized the social conditions of Ireland and given local control in local matters such as had not been known In a hundred years. There are three great questions before the Irish people, and this Unionist government-called into existence, as I repeat, because the Liberal party tried to pass home rule for Ireland-has dealt with two of them. First there was the question of the Irish university. The government appointed a commission of eminent educationists to inquire into the question and report. That report has been presented and, in due time, no doubt will be crystallized into law. They also passed a measure of local municipal government which will work out to the advantage of the people of Ireland and of the people of Great Britain. And to-day that government has presented a Bill in the Commons of Great Britain which will, for all time, redound to tl*e credit of all those who are responsible for it, and which proves beyond peradventure the desire of the Unionist government, if there is a grievance in Ireland respecting land tenure, to remove that grievance and give the tenantry of Ireland, who have such an intense love for the native land that they desire to cling to its soil and to eke out an existence even on small holdings, an opportunity of becoming landlords, which no government in ancient or modern times ever attempted to give to a people In a position similar to that of the Irish tenant farmers. These are proofs of the patriotism and desire to do justice to Ireland presented to the world by the Unionist government of Great Britain. These are proofs that the interests of Ireland are not being neglected, that the Unionist government have the interest of Ireland at heart and are giving practical proofs of their sympathy with Ireland by passing legislation which will undoubtedly redound to the peace and prosperity of that part of His Majesty's empire.
Sir, the Minister of Justice, just before he took his seat, made an admission which, I think, will not be questioned by any hon. gentleman who knows the facts and occupies a seat in this House. He said that up to the present time Ireland has been a hot bed of rebellion, a hot-bed of revolution. I would ask the hon. gentleman, would he think it the part of wisdom, if such a state of things existed in such an important, such an integral part of the United Kingdom, to pass a measure of local self-government that would satisfy the aspirations of the majority of the people among whom such a state of feeling exists ? The admission he has made is satisfactory proof to me that the action, up to the present time, of the government of the United Kingdom, has been wise, judicious and patriotic in the extreme. The Minister of Justice has not told us nor has any hon. gentleman who has spoken in this debate-the right hon. premier himself (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has not told us-of one disability, one grievance under which the Irish labour that the English and the Scotch and Welsh do not labour under as well. No hon. gentleman has pointed out a single disability existing ...in the south of Ireland that does not exist in the north as well. No hon. gentleman has pointed out one grievance that exists in Ulster that does not exist in Lancashire or in the counties north of the Tweed. There are no grievances in Ireland that are not common to the people of the United Kingdom. And where there are real grievances and they can be pointed out, the imperial parliament has proved its willingness and its desire to remove those grievances and to make the people united, contented, and prosperous, if it is possible to do so.
The hon. gentleman says that there are no grievances. Will he permit me to interrupt him ?
Yes.

Here is what Hon. T. W. Russell said a few days ago :
Conditions in Ireland are : Coercion revived, constitution suspended, public men in prison, landlordism supreme in Dublin castle, higher education hung up, parliament hamstrung, legislation impossible, people rushing from the country in tens of thousands to seek bread In foreign lands.
Does the hon. gentleman endorse that statement ?
The hon. gentleman says there are no grievances. Against his authority I put that of the Hon. T. W. Russell. That is all.

I should be very sorry indeed to set myself up as an authority against the gentleman whose opinion has been quoted. I do not know when that statement was made, or where it was made, but I will take the opportunity of reading a few lines from an official statement made by Mr. Russell before I take my seat. Now, Mr. Speaker, we have passed resolutions favouring home rule for Ireland on two or three occasions. I am not going to argue that matter now, because it has been argued in this parliament, which has passed these resolutions. I think, though, I might reiterate what has been said so well and so frequently during this debate, that we have quite a number of problems to solve ourselves, that we have a great deal to do in

this parliament, and we ought to occupy our time as far as available in the discharge of our duties in representing the Canadian people. We have no mandate from our constituents to express an opinion upon this abstract question of home rule for Ireland. What do they know about it ? They do not know any more about it than we do ourselves. Is it not rank impertinence, Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that 600 men, the chosen representatives of all parts of the United Kingdom meet from year to year, who have Ireland's condition and Ireland's grievances under their eyes all the time-is it not rank impertinence on our part to be intruding and protruding ourselves into the affairs of the United Kingdom and asking these 000 men to pass a measure of home rule for Ireland'/ Don't you think they know their own business better than we do ? It strikes me that it is reasonable to say they do. But let me go on. What have we done in parliament to aid Ireland by the passing of these resolutions, these empty, meaningless, impertinent resolutions ? We got snubbed for the first one we passed, and very properly so, snubbed by the Secretary for Colonial Affairs in the administration of the late Rt Hon. W. E. Gladstone, when we were told politely to mind our own business.
But, Mr. Speaker, a great deal of satisfaction has been taken in pointing out that since then we passed another resolution, practically unanimously, in 1899, I think, endorsing the imperial government respecting its action in the Transvaal and Orange River colonies. Is there no difference between passing this resolution favouring home rule for Ireland and our action in passing a resolution endorsing and approving the stand of the imperial government in demanding for British subjects in the Transvaal and Orange River colonies the rights that Irishmen enjoy in Ireland, and Scotchmen enjoy in Scotland ? Is there not a marked difference between the two resolutions ? In the one case we were reechoing the sentiments which found a place in the breasts of 999,000 out of every million people of the British empire ; we said to the mother land : We endorse your action, because you are demanding equal rights and fair play for the Uitlanders, which they do not get in a part of the world which is under the suzerainty of the British empire. Were we not right in taking that stand ? Is there any parallel, under the circumstances, in protruding ourselves upon the British parliament and demanding that Irish aspirations should be gratified by giving an independent legislature to that country, and say nothing about England, Scotland and Wales-or Ulster, for that matter, at the same time ? We have contented ourselves with passing these empty resolutions, while the imperial government has been at work, mitigating any wrong that exists, alleviating anything un-

toward that works harshly against the Irish people. What have we been doing ? Passing a resolution about once every seven years. About once in seven years the hon. member for Victoria, N.B. (Hon. Mr. Costi-gan) bobs up serenely and moves a resolution in favour of home rule for Ireland ; then we have a division on it, and prove that even the parliament of Canada is not a unit on this question, and he goes to sleep again for seven years. In the meantime the British government, this government that has been tyrannizing over Ireland for so many years, has been at work and we have been doing nothing.
Yes, Mr, Speaker, we have been doing something, and let me try to point out what we have done. We found that some time ago the imperial government placed an embargo on Canadian cattle, to the detriment of the Canadian producer and exporter. We did not stop to consider whether that embargo resulted advantageously to the Irish tenant farmer or not. We were so anxious to promote our own interests that we have been making representations to the imperial government asking that that embargo should be removed, asking that that keen competition, that fierce competition which the Irish tenant farmer has to encounter, encounter under great difficulties, encounter as a small holder of land, cultivating it under primitive methods-we are asking that that moderate measure of incidental protection which the embargo has given to the Irish tenant farmer should be removed, and that he should be obliged to meet us in open market in Liverpool, and compete with us for the sale of his store and fat cattle. If the hon. gentleman from Victoria had the interest of the Irish tenant farmer at heart, surely, Mr. Speaker, he would have raised his voice in favour of the maintenance of that embargo, and crown his life work in the promotion of Ireland's interests by securing for Ireland a measure of protection. I suppose that we will not hear the voice of the hon. gentleman raised in favour of the maintenance of that embargo during this session. I should hope that if he desired to secure for all time a record for consistency, he would insist that this embargo should remain where it is.
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that I think the hon. gentleman has been both consistent and persistent. Through evil report and good report, for twenty years he has brought up this home rule resolution. I merely point to the fact that it has been an empty thing, and that while something for the practical advantage of the tenant farmer might have been procured in this House, the hon. gentleman has not taken advantage of the occasion to do it. If he would use his great influence with his new found political allies, perhaps he might be able to get a genuine measure of preference for the poplins, for the laces, for the linens, in the manufacture of which the Irish people

excel. We have given tliem a so-called preference, and what does it amount to V We have only to read the record of the colonial conference to see what they think about the preference ; and if we have any doubt after reading the interpretation which the imperial officials put upon the value of that preference, we have only to read the instructions which have been issued by the Minister of Customs to the various collectors throughout this country to see what a sham that preference is, so far as advantage to the green isle is concerned. Might I ask my hon. friend, Mr. Speaker, after we have disposed of this resolution dealing with home rule, to turn his attention to that question of the preference ? Might I ask him again to use his influence, and I am sure he will have the co-operation of all Irishmen, whether they agree with him in regard to this resolution or not, in securing for the industrious workers of the Green Isle a real advantage, a real preference for their products in this fair land of Canada V He can do something practical for the Irish people by giving them a real and genuine preference for their products in the markets of the Dominion.
There is another way too, by which we might be of advantage to the Irish people. If we desire to show that we sympathize with them, if we desire to relieve them of a portion of the burden which rests heavily upon their shoulders, surely it would not be out of place in the day of our prosperity, in the day of our advancement, in this growing time for the hon. gentleman to propose that the time has come when it is expedient that this great young country of ours, full of boundless resources and having a future only limited by our appreciation of what we can make it should do something of substantial benefit for the Irish people. Surely we might expect from this hon. gentleman and those who sympathize with him that if they desire to be of real benefit to the Irish people, to the people of the north as well as to the people of the south, they would propose now that our coffers are overflowing, now that the money is pouring into the treasury of this Dominion of Canada-and we will support them in asking it- that a portion of that money should be sent to supplement the funds in the imperial exchequer for the maintenance of that peerless organization, the British navy, which protects our commerce in every nook and corner of the seven seas, that we might give a contribution towards the maintenance of the imperial navy which is to be found everywhere, and by such means we might relieve the Irish people of a portion of the burden which they are called upon to bear for the maintenance of that navy. I make these suggestions with all respect to the hon. member for Victoria, N.B., because these are practical ways in which he can benefit the Irish people, the minority as well as the majority, and he will find that 26
if he makes a motion of this kind he will have the cordial support and sympathy of those who regret that they cannot concur with him in the amendment which he has placed, Mr. Speaker, in your hands. I am afraid that I have taken up altogether too much of the time of the House and must apologize for having done so. During this afternoon we had the statement from the hon. member for Victoria, N.B., that the feeling in favour of home rule was growing steadily. I, with my hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes), believe that there is a great congestion of business in the imperial parliament. I often wonder how the imperial parliament discharges its duty as well as it does. I often wonder why it is that matters of detail, municipal matters, purely local matters are permitted to take up the time of the imperial parliament from day to day and year to year, and I hope to live to see the day come when some scheme will be adopted to relegate to the local authorities the right of dealing with these purely local matters. I want to see the Irish people given an opportunity, if they can agree upon th'e conditions, to govern, to a great extent, their local affairs, and I am satisfied that the people who are best qualified to bring about such a condition of things are the people of Ireland, of England and Scotland, represented in the imperial parliament, and I look upon our action in passing resolutions of this kind as rather a detriment than an advantage.
Just one or twoi words more before I sit down. I will only refer, very briefly, to what the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Costi-gan) has said. I dissent from his proposition that the feeling in favour of home rule, as it is understood by those who speak for the majority, is growing in England. Lord Rosebery represented Mr. Gladstone's government in the House of Lords when the Home Rule Bills were before the imperial parliament. Speaking on the 14th of February, 1902, at Liverpool, Lord Rosebery said :
The Irish leaders have demanded not what Mr. Gladstone was willing to give them, hut an independent parliament in Dublin.
Hon. gentlemen talk about giving to Ireland the same measure of self-government as we have in Canada. Those who profess to speak for the majority of the Irish people do not want provincial autonomy such as we enjoy in the provinces of Canada; they want complete autonomy, they want legislative independence, they want that and they will not be satisfied with anything else. That is the opinion of Lord Rosebery, one of the members of Mr. Gladstone's cabinet who supported his leader In advocating and presenting that measure of home rule that met with disaster on two occasions -in the imperial parliament. Let me repeat again i what Lord Rosebery says :



The Irish leaders have demanded not what Mr. Gladstone was willing to give them, but an independent parliament in Dublin. Now, when you get there, I say, ' Halt ' ! I am not prepared at any time or under any circumstances to grant an independent parliament in Dublin.
I need not point out to lion, members on both sides of the House the prominent position which Lord Rosebery occupies in the public eye of the United Kingdom. He is a keen observer of current events and I think his opinion of the attitude, the demands and the requirements of the leaders of the home rule party is entitled to some consideration at the hands of the Canadian parliament; and I say that his statement that the home rule leaders have changed their position is a statement that cannot be successfully controverted by any hon. member of this House, if the leaders of the home rule party are held responsible for the public utterances they have made, or for what they say from day to day, from week to week and from year to year in addressing their constituents and the people of the United Kingdom. But, Sir, let me read the opinion of another hon. gentleman, a gentleman who is highly thought of and deservedly so, who is acclaimed by Irish Catholics and Protestants alike, a gentleman who speaks for the government of which he is a member, whose heroism, whose courage and whose patriotism in preparing and presenting the measure of land reform which is now before the imperial parliament has challenged the admiration of the British people. I refer to the Right Hon. Geo. Wyndham. In a speech made in March last, in Liverpool, I think it was, although I am not sure, he made this statement:
What are the facts that stand out from the midst of the constitutional problem involved in the Irish question ? They are these : Mr. Gladstone's bills are dead-dead on their merits. They never had been accepted by England. They would have brought Ireland to bankruptcy within a very few years. In the second place, an independent parliament for Ireland is an impossibility ; and in the third place, (he common exchequer of the two countries will never be divided	
These are strong utterances from a responsible minister and a member of a powerful government that is proving its desire to help Ireland by the legislation which it has enacted and which it is enacting.
To sum up this constitutional argument which has recently been reopened, these two islands, by the inflexible ordinance of geography, of history and of finance are bound, and must ever be bound together by ties even closer than those which bind our colonies to the mother country.
These are the expressions of two men occupying prominent positions in the public life of the United Kingdom, and I take it that their utterances are worthy of some consideration and should have some value attached to them in the parliament of Canada. I promised the hon. Minister of Jus-

tice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) that I would read three or four words from the statement of a gentleman whom he quoted-Mr. T. W. Russell. I quote from the ' Daily Mail ' Year-book. He says :
There is, first of all, what I may call the national demand for the restoration of rights taken away by the Act of Union. Historically, the demand has its origin in the fact that the Act of Union was carried by means which could not be adopted to-day. And the overwhelming majority of the Irish people take Lord Plunkett's view that the Act and the whole proceedings connected with it were ultra vires.
The British people, however, have had an opportunity of reconsidering the question. All the facts-thanks to Mr. Gladstone-were put before the public mind, and Ireland's demand for the restoration of a native legislature was refused. This refusal does not alter feeling in Ireland. It probably renders it more bitter.
I desire to draw the attention of lion, gentlemen to this particular part of the statement :
But it does remove the question somewhat out of the region of practical politics in Great Britain. Still the home rule question is far from being dead. And the people who imagine a vain thing may some day or other have a sudden and rude awakening.
This is the statement Mr. T. W. Russell makes with regard to the position which the home rule question occupies in imperial politics to-day. The right hon. leader of the House in his eloquent address to-night, pledging his support to the resolution, touched the crucial point when he observed that mistrust and lack of confidence was one of the main causes for the refusal of the minority in Ireland to agree to the establishment of a native parliament. Are the minority Justified in holding that view ? Are they justified in withholding their assent from such a measure ? They are, Mr. Speaker, amply justified because the history of the past twenty-five years teems with evidence of the disloyalty of those who have been advocating home rule, and declaration after declaration has been made by these men; declarations that cannot be misconstrued; that the goal they are reaching for is not provincial autonomy such as we enjoy in Canada, but absolute separation and the establishment of a separate parliament for Ireland. Sir, I need not say to you or to any gentleman in this House, that that separate parliament cannot be granted. Certainly it never can be granted, as long as one-fourth of the people of the Green Isle, the minority-whose very existence, whoso attainment of prosperity gives the lie to the statement that Ireland labours under disabilities and disadvantages-I say that this measure for a native parliament can never become an accomplished fact until the majority by their actions prove to the minority, that they have been saying what they do not mean; that they desire to live in peace and amity and concord with the minority and to give that minority absolute equality and every measure of protection

that the majority desire for themselves. The right hon. the premier quoted from utterances given expression to by Mr. Dillon some years ago. Let me quote for the right hon. gentleman some of the language which Mr. John Dillon has used within the past twelve months. Speaking at Liverpool on March 12th, 1902, Mr. John Dillon said :
He promised Lord Rosebery and Lord Salisbury that as long as Ireland was denied that God-given right of freedom-a right for which men ought to fight if they could-they would never be loyal.
At Greenock on March 14tli, 1902, Mr. Dillon said :
If they had the power to-morrow they would be the greatest cowards in the world to submit to English government if they were able to overthrow it with physicial force.
Does my right hon. friend wonder that the prosperous, the contented, the progressive minority in Ireland object to have their affairs administered by men who give utterance to such expressions ? Does the right hon. gentleman wonder that under these circumstances there is a sharp line of distinction drawn between those who are prosperous and loyal and those who are disaffected and discontented; and will not my right hon. friend admit that every vestige of suspicion, every vestige of mistrust that exists in the mind of the minority must be removed before any local government can be granted that will be workable in Ireland? I have quoted from the statements made by Mr. John Dillon. Let me quote from the statement of a gentleman occupying a still more prominent position in the home rule party. I refer to Mr. John Redmond, M.P. On the 20th of October, 1901, at Maryborough, Queen's county, on a Sunday, Mr. John Redmond made this statement:
I point to what is going on in Connaught as an example to the rest of Ireland. If only all over Ireland to-day we had as vigorous and-I won't mince words-as dangerous a movement as there exists at this moment in Connaught, we would make short work of the land question and short work, as I believe, of the English government of our country (cheers).
My one principle in public life is-in every department of the government, from the highest to the lowest-from the chief secretary in his back room in Dublin castle down to the landgrabber and the bailiff in the country town-to make every department of government In this country difficult and dangerous (cheers). That has always been my principle in public life. I have made no disguise of it. I have said it over and over again in the House of Commons.-* Freeman's ' Journal, October 21, 1901.
Does the right hon. leader of this House wonder, when the leader of the home rule movement within the last fifteen months gave expressions to such views as this, that he does not enjoy to the extent he ought to enjoy it, if home rule is to be a success, the sympathy and confidence of the minority of the people of the Green Isle ? Mr. Redmond came to America on a mission.
26}
Before he sailed on the evening of October 22, 1901, he arrived in Cork, accompanied by Mr. P. A. McHugh, M.P., and Mr. Thomas O'Donnell, M.P. Addressing a large gathering in front of the Victoria hotel, Mr. Redmond explained his mission to America. He said :
It means that the reunion which has taken place in Ireland has taken place also in America ; it means that those English statesmen- shallow, short-sighted men, who imagined that because we were torn with dissention here for the last ten years that the cause of Ireland was dead and buried-it means that these men will understand when they see this mission to America that they have to fight against a united Irish race who are simply united by one consideration to use whatever means are honourable and just in the sight of God, and who care nothing for English law (cheers), and who are prepared to say before the world that, rather than be held by force, as we are to-day, under the British empire, we would prefer to be linked with the meanest free country on the face of the earth.
I am going to our race in America to ask them for their sympathy, to ask them for their support, and to tell them that, in my honest belief, we are near the day when England will be weak and degraded (cheers), when oppressed nationalities will be strong, and when Ireland's support may be a matter of vital consequence to English statesmen and English parties (renewed cheering). But this mission to America has another meaning that I would commend to the minds of those English newspapers that are curious and anxious upon the subject. To-day England stands alone in the world ; to-day the public opinion of every civilized nation is against England ; and one of my objects in going to America is to prove to English statesmen that the public opinion of the world is against England and is upon the side of Ireland (cheers), that the whole public opinion of the American nation, of the leading statesmen, and of all political parties is in complete sympathy with Ireland's demand for freedom ; and that is another meaning of this mission. It will show to England that she will have to count in the future on a united Irish race of twenty millions throughout the world, backed by the public opinion, the sympathy, and the support of over seventy millions.-** Freeman's Journal,' October 23, 1901.
That extract is from the ' Freeman's Journal ' of October 23, 1901. But Mr. Redmond said something more, and I would not trespass on the time of the House at such length except for the prominent position he occupies in the home rule party. Several addresses including those from the Cork Eviction Tenants' Association and the Cork Trades Council were presented to Mr. Redmond! just on the eve of his departure and in reply he said :
I have no hesitation in saying that the United Irish League stands to-day precisely on the same foundation as stood the Land League when Parnell declared he would never take off his coat in the movement if there was not behind the agrarian movement the national question (applause). This United Irish League Is not merely an agrarian movement. It is first, last, and all the time a national movement (applause); and those of us who are endeavour-

ing to rouse the farmers of Ireland, as we endeavoured twenty years ago in the days of the Land League to rouse them, are doing so not merely to obtain the removal of their particular grievances, but because we believe by rousing them we will be strengthening the national movement and helping us to obtain our end, which is, after all, the national independence of Ireland.
That is the statement of this gentleman, and he adds :
I desire to say to the tradesmen of Ireland that I hope they will not be led away by these enemies of the Irish movement who are endeavouring to induce them to think that this is a purely agrarian movement. It is nothing of the kind. It is a national movement, having for its first and last object the emancipation of Ireland as a nation.-' Freeman's Journal,' October 24, 1901.
1 do not know whether the hon. gentleman meant what he said or not ; but if he meant what he said, do you wonder that those who desire for themselves and for those who come after them, a continuance of privileges which they now enjoy as British subjects, shall not have their interests confided to men who hold such sentiments as those I have read ? Do you wonder that a minority of, the people of Ireland, who are contented and prosperous, desire that the status quo shall be maintained, rather than that they should be led into an enterprise that would bring them into opposition to England and Scotland, and to their sons and brothers across the channel ? Mr. Redmond was the principal speaker at a large meeting in the Rotunda in Dublin, when a letter from Mr. Wm, O'Brien was read, in which he said :
In thanking you for your kind invitation, allow me to express the hope that, if the English King carries out his threatened visit to Ireland next year, the United Irish League in Dublin will succeed in rousing such a spirit as will convince His Majesty from the hour he lands that he comes amongst a people discontented and disaffected to the core, who only need the arms and training of the Boers to testify their hatred of England's rule, with an eloquence equal to that of the unconquered South African Republics.
I leave these extracts from the speeches and letters of the men who are the leaders of this home rule movement, with hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, and I ask them how they can wonder that the minority who have done their full share in maintaining the prestige and extending the influence and the power of the British empire, and whose sons have held their own in Ireland and everywhere else throughout the world, protest emphatically against the passage of any measure by the imperial parliament that would lessen or weaken the ties which now happily unite the people of Ireland with the people of England and Scotland. The minority in Ireland are able to take care of themselves; they have always done so ; and the condition of the north of Ireland to-day proves conclusively that

people may live in Ireland in contentment and prosperity under the rule that now exists. The prosperous condition of the city of Belfast and the districts surrounding it, teeming with an industrial population, employed at good wages, is a proof that there is nothing incompatible with progress and prosperity in Ireland for those who are industrious and willing to work and who will put their shoulders to the wheel to promote the best material interests of their native land. This minority have sent to Canada as their contribution to the public life of this country since confederation such men as Monck, Lisgar, Dufferin and Lansdowne. They have given to the empire their share of the empire's soldiers and sailors, and they have been proud to fight side by side and shoulder to shoulder with their fellow-countrymen who worship at a different altar. They desire to live on terms of peace, amity and concord with those who comprise the majority. They desire to unite with them cordially and heartily in promoting every measure which shall be for the advancement of their native land. They have the right to speak for Ireland as well as the majority. They comprise 1,150,000 in a population of 4,458,000 in Ireland. These people have a right to have their views considered by hon. gentlemen on both sides of this House. If time permitted, I could read resolutions passed in the chambers of commerce of Dublin and Belfast by the men who are foremost in promoting the industrial interests of Ireland, denouncing home rule and expressing their desire to continue to enjoy their full measure of citizenship in the British empire. I could read the memorials submitted to the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland by the representatives of the Church of England in Ireland, numbering G00.000, the Presbyterians, Methodists and other nonconformist bodies, aggregating 1,100,000 people, in the same sense ; but I do not wish to take up the time of the House. Putting the question on the lowest ground, I say that if these people who live under such happy conditions in Ireland thought that their personal and material welfare would be promoted by such a measure of home rule as is proposed, they certainly would he amongst the foremost to demand it. But they believe that they enjoy greater privileges, immunities and blessings, and have greater opportunities for preferment, by remaining an integral part of the empire; and for that reason, and also because they have no confidence in those who represent the majority in Ireland, they have set their faces as steel against home rule. Have we in this parliament any right to pass this resolution without considering the position that minority occupy ? The difficulty and the dilemma which the minority may find themselves in to-day or to-morrow in Ireland because of the passing of such resolutions a? that proposed by the hon. member for Victoria, may be the difficulty and the dil-

emma of the minority in Canada to-morrow. That minority only ask to be left alone. They live under less favourable conditions than the people of the southern and eastern parts of Ireland; yet they have proved their capacity to advance and prosper; and all we ask on their behalf is that their views shall be heard, and that this House shall not pass any resolution which will place the people of Canada and the people of Ireland in a false position. There are other ways in which we can'i give substantial assistance to the heavily-burdened taxpayers of England, Ireland and Scotland. Let us do something practical. Resolutions of this kind practically amount to nothing. They will not influence a vote in the parliament of the United Kingdom. The people in that parliament know their duty and are always prepared to do it; and instead of promoting the welfare and peace and integrity of Ireland, and the influence which Canada ought to possess in the councils of the empire, the passage of this resolution will place the people of Ireland and the people of Canada in a false light. I feel it my duty to record my vote against the resolution, because I think it is ill-timed and will serve no good purpose.

I would not have said anything on this question, Mr. Speaker, had it not been for a remark that was dropped by the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) to the effect that those who vote against this resolution have no sympathy for Ireland. I wish to say that like the hon. gentleman I belong to a third generation of Irishmen. My forefathers, as far back as I can remember, have all been Irishmen, and I want to say that they have been loyal Irishmen. They have done in their day fighting enough, I think, to satisfy the next twenty generations of Ingrams in this country. One of my forefathers resided in the city of Quebec many years ago. He was sent to Canada by the British government with other soldiers to defend the flag at Quebec. Therefore, I do not take any back seat in regard for the interests of Ireland. Before coming to attend this session of parliament I was requested to support a home rule resolution that was to be introduced into this House. I asked by whom the resolution would be introduced. I was told by the Hon. John Costigan. I said immediately that I would neither support such a resolution nor any other piece of legislation which the Hon. John Costigan might introduce. I would oppose this motion or any other piece of legislation introduced by the Hon. John Costigan into this House. That may not be a very convincing answer, but I assure my hon. friend that it is eminently in fitting with the motives which prompted the mover of this resolution. I know that nothing would delight the hon. gentleman more than for hon. members of this House to heap on his head a great amount of abuse, but I
j want to point to a fact by which we can gauge the honesty of the hon. gentleman. He took occasion to take up a considerable time of the House in proclaiming his own honesty. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is a well known maxim that whenever a man boasts of his honesty, you should keep your hand very tightly on your pocket. This hon. gentleman has told us to-day that his honesty has been exceedingly great within the last twenty years. But he failed to dwell on a little incident to which I shall recall to the attention of the House. A few years ago, when the Conservative party were in power, there was a very live issue agitating the people and provoking considerable discussion in this House and country. I refer to the Manitoba school question. The hon. gentleman professed then, as he does now, to be the great advocate of the interests of the Roman Catholics of this country. He was a member of the Conservative government of that day, and then as now he was more useful once every seven years or so promoting a resolution of this kind than in doing anything else. What did he then do ? He was then advocating remedial legislation. Some difficulty arose in the Conservative administration, Sir Mackenzie Bowell, the Prime Minister, resigned, and Sir Charles Tupper was called on to assume the leadership of the party. What did we find the hon. gentleman doing ? When asked to take a seat in the cabinet under Sir Charles Tupper, he wrote a letter to Sir Charles, in which he used these words
In view, however, of the principle involved in remedial legislation, to which Sir Mackenzie Howell's government was pledged
I rise to a point of order. On a motion in favour of home rule the hon. gentleman is not warranted in discussing the Manitoba school question.
I presume that I am as much in order as the hon. gentleman was when he brought us to South Africa. I am dealing with a question affecting Canada, which is more than the hon. gentleman did.
I would call attention to the fact that we are now discussing the question of home rule, and would invite the hon. gentleman to confine his remarks to this question.

I shall try and do so. I was going on to quote this letter, and if you have no objection, Mr. Speaker, I will finish the quotation
- and In view of the fact that your government Is to be formed to carry out the same policy, especially as regards the Manitoba school policy, I feel it my duty to say to you at once that you may count upon my assistance and services if you require them, as a member of your government, always presuming that the policy to reintroduce a remedial Bill at the first session of the new parliament will be clearly announced by you on behalf of your government.

What I wish to point out is that if the hon. gentleman had been honest then, he would not, after Sir Charles Tupper had gone to the country and been defeated on this very question, have turned his back on his leader and been the means of wrecking his government. Why, when a man for eighteen long years has been a member of the cabinet-I care not whether a Liberal or a Conservative government-and then takes the stand which the hon. gentleman did, I say that he can have no pretense to honesty or decency.
Order.
I must ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw the expression.

I of course shall bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker. The hon. gentleman spoke of his unselfishness and his strong convictions, but it occurred to me that these convictions could not have been very strong at the time to which I refer. I would like to know from the hon. gentleman to-night whether it is not a fact that last session he was going to introduce his home rule resolution, and that the right hon. the First Minister persuaded him not to do so.
It is not a fact.

Will the hon. gentleman say who did ? If he wishes to be honest, I pause to give him an opportunity to reply. He does not choose to avail himself of that opportunity. Let me repeat that the hon. gentleman fully intended to introduce this resolution last session, but failed to do so. Why ? Because there was a likelihood of an election in the province of Ontario, and the introduction of that resolution last session would have been the means perhaps of defeating the government. My hon. friend was quite ready to kick this resolution around like a football so long as he could serve party purposes. Reference has been made to the cattle embargo. Well, not long ago on the motion to go into supply, an hon. member introduced a resblution respecting the cattle embargo in England. But he had hardly moved his motion when the hon. Minister of Finance called upon his majority to vote it down as a motion of want of confidence. Does not that prove conclusively that the hon. member for Victoria (Hon. Mr. Costigan) and the government have been in collusion on this question for the purpose of making political capital and nothing else. There is another question on which I desire to speak, because it is one that has some relation to home rule. A few years ago when in this House the question of provincial autonomy for the Northwest Territories was being discussed, not one of the government supporters rose to assist the members of the opposition in their advocacy of provincial autonomy in the North-west. Not one of them rose to take an active part in that discussion. I am Mr. INGRAM.
therefore justified in saying to them that if they would pay a little more attention to our own affairs in Canada instead of taking up this home rule question for the sole purpose of gaining political notoriety and support, they would be giving more evidence of sincerity and honesty than they are now doing. I do not intend taking up any more time. I simply rose to say that although I have in my time supported home rule resolutions and would support them again today, I will never support any resolution in favour of home rule so long as it is introduced by a gentleman whom I despise for his conduct in this House, and for the motives which actuate his present course. I am using strong language, Mr. Speaker, but not any stronger than the occasion warrants and demands, and I think the sooner the people of this country understand it the better. I should have been glad to support the resolution had it been moved by the Minister of Justice or some other Irishman in this country who is not trading in this class of goods for political purposes.
